catalog_quote: Phonologically, Tiddim Chin has three contrastive tones with relatively complex tone sandhi, as well as several intonation patterns. ... As shown in Table 3, Tiddim Chin has three distinctive tones: a rising tone, a level tone, and a falling tone. The pitch of each tone varies according to vowel length and the sonority of a syllable-final consonant. ... 2.2 Syllable structure Tiddim Chin's syllable structure can be reduced to (C1) (V1) V2 (V3) (C2) / T, where C1 represents an onset consonant, V represents a vowel, C2 represents a coda consonant, and T represents a tone. Each syllable consists of a vowel and may include an onset and a coda. A majority of Tiddim Chin morphemes are phonologically monosyllabic (e.g., nê¹ "eat"), though a few show a disyllabic combination of two monosyllabic structures (e.g., pa³tâu³ "nervous"). ... new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Katsura 1964, p. 30 ( lines 135-152 and 171-174): the compiler reported no tone/accent terms in the scanned, but the paper explicitly describes Tiddim Chin tonemes (トネーム) with three types, 平板型 level, 上昇型 rising, 下降型 falling (examples ta:i 'flee' level vs ta:i 'scold' rising; sun 'stab' and su:n 'afternoon' falling), and says the missionary romanisation marks none of them; §3 says the phoneme and toneme system was worked out from a ~600-word list. This is a tone statement, not a stress statement, so it changes the per-work reading (none found -> tone language, no stress statement) but not the relation to the catalog (silent). No work marked silent says anything about word stress or accent.

Stopped syllables with syllable weight not falling directly on the vowel are generally not tone bearing units; their pitch tends to approximate that of TC-III. ... 1.3.3 Tone Category III This is attested as a falling tone in all the languages which concurs nicely with its historical source proposed in 5.3. ... it sometimes appears to approximate the contour of Tedim TC-III which conversely has a sandhi variant, noted by Luce (1962:11), that parallels the Zo contour.

sources.citation: Ostapirat, Weera. 1998. Tiddim Chin tones in historical perspective. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 21(1): 235-248. doi:10.32655/ltba.21.1.06
sources.quote: 'Tiddim Chin shows three tones in smooth syllables (syllables ending with sonorants and vowels): rising, level and falling, which are numbered by Henderson (1965) as tones 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Long checked syllables ... also occur with these three tones. Short checked syllables only occur with a low level tone, which has been considered to be an allotone of tone 3.' No mention of word stress/accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent scanned: 'stress'/'accent'/'promin' occur only in non-prosodic senses).
